The City of San Marino appreciates your attendance. Citizens’ interest provides the Council with
valuable information regarding issues of the community.

Regular meetings are held on the 2nd Wednesday of every month at 6:00 p.m. Typically, adjourned

In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act, any person with a disability who requires

MOTION TO WAIVE FURTHER READINGS

This action permits the City Council to act on ordinances and resolutions without having to read
the entire text of the ordinance or resolution. The title of an ordinance on First Reading must
be read in its entirety. An ordinance on Second Reading does not require having the title read.
However, the City Council may request that an ordinance or resolution be read in its entirety
before taking any action.

BY:  Steve A. Filarsky, Labor Relations Counsel

DATE:  November 17, 2021

SUBJECT:  ADOPTION OF RESOLUTION NO. R-21-28, IMPLEMENTING A
  MANDATORY  VACCINE MANDATE  FOR  EMPLOYEES
  REPRESENTED BY THE SAN MARINO FIREFIGHTERS
  ASSOCIATION ("SMFFA")

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

x Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
x Safe Community
x Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

The San Marino Firefighters Association (SMFFA) is the exclusive representative for non-
management classifications in the City’s Fire Department, including Firefighter/Paramedics, Fire
Engineers, and Fire Captains. The City requires employees in all classifications to maintain their
Paramedic certification. The City and SMFFA are subject to a current Memorandum of
Understanding, which is set to expire on June 30, 2022.

The COVID-19 pandemic began spreading into the United States in early 2020, with increasing
speed in March 2020. On March 4, 2020, Governor Newsom declared a state of emergency in
California. On March 19, 2020, Governor Newsom issued an Executive Order, instituting a
shelter-in-place mandate statewide with limited exceptions. While the State entered a multi-
tier reopening stage in mid-2020, a seasonal surge in case infection and hospitalization rates in
late 2020 led Governor Newsom to impose a limited stay at home order on November 16,
2020.

The FDA provided emergency use authorization to three different vaccines against COVID-19
in late 2020. Starting in early 2021, individuals in California began receiving applicable doses of
one of the three FDA-approved COVID-19 vaccines. The decision to obtain a COVID-19
vaccine remained voluntary at that time.

  Page 5 of 30
 In the summer of 2021, several factors led government agencies and public health authorities to
reconsider whether to adopt mandatory COVID-19 vaccination mandates. Among others, a
persistent variant of the initial COVID-19 virus (the “Delta variant”) emerged, which led to an
increase in case infection rates - among vaccinated persons, and particularly among
unvaccinated persons.

On August 12, 2021, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health (“LACDPH”) issued
a Public Health Order ("Order"), imposing a requirement that covered employees either
provide proof of COVID-19 vaccination or obtain a limited exemption by September 30, 2021.
The Order applies to a variety of employees providing healthcare services, including
“paramedics.” The Order provides an exemption for employees who object based on
“religious beliefs” or have a “qualifying medical reason.”

The City concluded that the August 12 LACDPH Order applied to represented employees in
these SMFFA represented classifications, and required the City to either: (i) obtain proof of
their vaccination status by September 30, 2021 or (ii) when appropriate, provide religious or
disability exemptions by September 30, and begin enforcing face covering and weekly testing
protocols at that time for those with valid exemptions.

On August 19, 2021, Scott Pilch, the City’s then-Human Resources Manager, invited the union
to engage in bargaining on the negotiable "effects" 1 of the Order. Fire Chief Mario Rueda
followed up by email with SMFFA, advising that the Order applied to its members. The parties
thereafter met on five occasions between late August 2021 and early October 2021 to discuss
the “effects” of the Order as well as the City’s proposed policy.

On September 24, 2021, the statewide Firefighters organization issued a "Legal Memo to Local
Affiliates" (including SMFFA) stating in part:

  "Employees are not being forced to take the vaccine. They can freely choose
  not to take the vaccine. Moreover, the employer is not testing the vaccine on its
  employees. Human testing occurred before the vaccine was authorized for
  emergency use. Pfizer and other pharmaceutical companies tested vaccines on
  human subjects. Those human subjects gave their consent to be tested. An
  example of forced human testing would look like the following: co-workers
  come into your office, hold you down, and jab you with the vaccine without
  consent. That is not happening here. Your employer is mandating the vaccine
  to keep others safe. If you do not want to take the vaccine, you do not have to
  take the vaccine. However, the employer may terminate you because you are
  not abiding by the conditions of your employment." (emphasis added) 2

1
 The "decision" to implement a mandatory vaccine policy is outside the scope of representation, University of
California (2021) PERB Decision No. 2783-H.
2
  The full memorandum is included here as Attachment 2.

  Page 6 of 30
 On October 4, 2021, the City verbally declared an impasse in negotiations over the vaccine
mandate. On October 7, 2021, the City confirmed the impasse in writing. The City's impasse
procedure is set forth in Sections 18.14 and 18.15 of the City's Personnel Rules. Section
18.15(A) provides:

  "Either party may request in writing of the other party no more than ten (10)
  calendar days following the agreement that an impasse exists, that advisory
  arbitration be entered into."

SMFFA made no such request.

In 2011 the California Legislature implemented "fact-finding" for agencies (such as the City)
subject to the Meyers-Milias-Brown Act (Government Code Section 3500, et. seq.)
Government Code Section 3505.4 provides in part:

  "If the dispute was not submitted to mediation, an employee organization may
  request that the parties’ differences be submitted to a factfinding panel not later
  than 30 days following the date that either party provided the other with a
  written notice of a declaration of impasse."

SMFFA made no such request.

DISCUSSION

Having exhausted the meet and confer process, and SMFFA waiving any post-impasse
procedure (both advisory arbitration and fact-finding), it is now appropriate that City Council
unilaterally implement a mandatory City vaccine policy for SMFFA that does not provide for
ongoing testing and masking for those who voluntarily choose not to get vaccinated (absent a
valid medical or religious exemption).

The practical consequence is that there is a single employee in SMFFA who remains
unvaccinated. It is recommended that this City policy go into effect on Tuesday, November 23,
2021. This will allow the one remaining employee one final opportunity to get vaccinated
rather than be terminated.

Attached is a Resolution for your adoption.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

None.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City’s Labor Counsel drafted this report and approves it as to form.

  Page 7 of 30
 RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the City Council adopt the attached Resolution, "Implementation of a
Mandatory Vaccine Mandate for Employees Represented by the San Marino Firefighters
Association." If the City Council concurs with staff’s recommendation, an appropriate motion
would be:

“I move to adopt Resolution No. R-21-28, "Implementation of a Mandatory Vaccine Mandate
for Employees Represented by the San Marino Firefighters Association.”

ATTACHMENTS

1. Resolution No. R-21-28
2. Legal Memorandum to Local Affiliates from California Professional Firefighters

  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED:

1.  Effective Tuesday, November 23, 2021, a mandatory City COVID-19 vaccine policy shall
  be implemented for employees represented by SMFFA.

2.  Absent a valid medical or religious exemption that can be accommodated by the City,
  regular testing and masking is not a substitute for vaccination.

3.  Employees who fail to comply with this City vaccine mandate shall be separated from
  employment.

4.  The City Manager is directed to provide written notice to all SMFFA employees of this
  mandatory City COVID-19 vaccination policy.

Hi Team,

As mentioned on our call today, here is some information about vaccine case law and
requirements as shared by CPF.

  BELOW IS THE LEGAL MEMO TO LOCAL AFFILIATES:

  DATE:  September 24, 2021

  TO:  CPF Affiliate Leaders

  RE:  COVID-19 VACCINATIONS

  With the recent rise in COVID-19 cases, states are mandating public employees to either get vaccinated or
  submit to regular COVID-19 testing. President Biden announced a similar vaccine mandate for all federal
  workers. Law firms have fielded multiple inquiries about your employers mandating the vaccine. The first
  question is: Can you be terminated if you refuse to get the vaccine? The short answer is yes. Law firms will
  face an uphill battle trying to defeat vaccine mandates because vaccine mandates have been legal since
  the beginning of the 20th Century. This letter addresses the current law on vaccine mandates and related
  issues.

  States/Local Governments Can Mandate Vaccinations

  Over 100 years ago, the Supreme Court decided that states can mandate that their citizens get vaccinated.
  In Jacobson v. Commonwealth of Massachusetts (1905) 197 U.S. 11, the Court upheld a local law in
  Cambridge, Massachusetts requiring inhabitants receive the smallpox vaccine. The Court’s ruling relied on
  the principles that an individual’s right to liberty and bodily autonomy is not absolute, and that states have
  the authority to take actions necessary to protect the health and wellbeing of their citizens (commonly
  referred to as states’ “police powers”).

  The Supreme Court did not revisit government mandated vaccinations again until 1922 in Zucht v.
  King(1922) 260 U.S. 174. The Zucht Court held that mandating vaccines for only one group of people (in
  this case school children), did not violate individuals’ Fourteenth Amendment rights to due process or equal
  protection. This same logic would likely apply to a mandate that first responders or public safety officers be
  vaccinated, even if the same requirement is not applied to the general public.

  On August 12, 2021, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Barrett refused to block Indiana State University’s COVID-
  19 vaccine mandate. (Docket No. 21A15). Eight students sought an emergency appeal of a ruling upholding

  Page 13 of 30
 the efficacy of Jacobson. Klaassen v. Trustees of Indiana University (7th Cir., Aug. 2, 2021, No. 21-2326)
2021 WL 3281209. Interestingly, the Seventh Circuit noted “this case is easier than Jacobson for the
University, for two reasons.” First, Jacobson sustained a vaccination requirement without any exceptions
for adults, whereas the university permitted religious and medical exceptions. Second, the mandate did not
apply to the entire public, but was only a condition of attending the university. The Court further noted that
universities have many conditions of enrollment that individuals may not like, and students who do not
wish to be vaccinated have ample educational opportunities elsewhere.

Multiple California appellate courts have upheld Jacobson and Zucht, ruling that when it comes to
mandatory vaccinations, finding the need for public safety outweighs individuals’ rights to privacy or bodily
autonomy. In Brown v. Smith (2018) 24 Cal.App.5th 1135 and Love v. State Dept. of Education (2018) 29
Cal.App.5th 980, California appellate courts upheld Senate Bill No. 277, which repealed the personal belief
exemption to California’s immunization requirements for school children. Thus, the courts limited the
exemptions available (once full FDA approval is received) to: 1) a sincerely held religious belief, practice or
observation; or 2) a medical accommodation.

In the Texas case Bridges v. Houston Methodist Hospital (S.D. Tex., June 12, 2021, No. CV H-21-1774)
2021 WL 2399994, Houston Methodist Hospital implemented a policy requiring staff to be vaccinated or
face termination. A number of employees sued claiming wrongful termination after they refused to be
vaccinated. The court cited Jacobson as proof that an employer can mandate vaccines. The court also
dismissed the employees’ arguments that the COVID-19 vaccine was distinguishable because it had only
received “emergency” approval. The court concluded: “Bridges can freely choose to accept or refuse a
COVID-19 vaccine; however, if she refuses, she will simply need to work somewhere else... Every
employment includes limits on the worker's behavior in exchange for his remuneration. That is all part of
the bargain.” (Id. at p. *2.) It is important to note that this case dealt with a private employer. However,
the rationale is applicable to public employers and employees.

California courts will most likely uphold COVID-19 vaccine mandates as well. In December 2020, the
Alameda County Superior Court upheld the University of California’s flu vaccine mandate because it was
“narrowly tailored” to reduce transmission of the flu. The court reiterated that there was no case in which a
court struck down a mandatory vaccine imposed as a condition of attending school or college, as a
condition of access to property for the purpose of employment, or as violating bodily autonomy.

It is well-settled law that governments can mandate that employees be vaccinated. However, this authority
is not absolute. Government employers may still be required to make accommodations for people with
medical conditions that make vaccination a risk or for people with sincere religious beliefs. These narrow
exemptions are discussed below.

Medical Exemption

An individual that suffers adverse medical consequences—such as an allergic reaction—to vaccinations may
be entitled to a reasonable accommodation under the ADA and FEHA.

The ADA and FEHA require that employers provide a reasonable accommodation for an employee’s
disability. The employee must first put their employer on notice and request accommodation to begin an
interactive process. In addition, employees must put forward medical documentation to substantiate their
claim of a disability.

Religious Exemption

  Page 14 of 30
 Individuals with sincerely held religious objections to the COVID-19 vaccine may also seek a religious
accommodation to a vaccination requirement under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and FEHA.

An employer must make reasonable accommodations for employees sincerely held religious beliefs unless
an employer demonstrates that he is unable to reasonably accommodate… without undue hardship on the
conduct of the employer’s business. Thus, an employer is obligated to try to reasonably accommodate an
employee’s religious beliefs to the extent it does not cause an undue hardship on the business, and failure
to do so violates Title VII and FEHA. This does not mean that the employer is required to offer an
employee their preferred accommodation. Rather, the accommodation offered simply must be reasonable.
Thus, if the employee does not accept the reasonable accommodation, the employee may be terminated.

Right to Bargain Over the Impacts and Effects of Mandatory Vaccinations

While mandating vaccination is legal, the impacts and effects of such a decision fall within the scope of
bargaining. PERB recently held the decision to adopt an influenza vaccination policy was outside the scope
of representation because the need to protect public health was not amenable to collective bargaining or,
alternatively, outweighed the benefits of bargaining over the policy. However, the University’s
implementation of the vaccination policy constituted a unilateral change, in violation of HEERA, because the
University was not privileged to implement the policy before completing negotiations over its effects.
(Regents of the University of California (2021) PERB Decision No. 2783-H.) The University had not met and
conferred in good faith before implementation of the policy.

Labor leaders should demand to bargain over the impacts and effects of any vaccination policy. And, if the
failure to get vaccinated could lead to discipline, the policy itself may be subject to decision bargaining.
Employers must provide notice and opportunity to meet and confer prior to mandating vaccines.

A reasonable notice is one where the employer clearly, in writing, describes its vaccination policy and
clearly informs the union of the nature, scope, and timing of the implementation of the policy. The union
must then clearly and unequivocally invoke its right to bargain and set forth the negotiable impacts and
effects of the policy.

Potential negotiable subjects include the following: 1) the payment of vaccine costs for employees who do
not have insurance; 2) the availability of vaccine clinics; 3) alternatives to unpaid leave or discipline as
consequences for not getting vaccinated; 4) timing concerning the enforcement of the prohibition on
access to worksites and facilities for employees who had not complied; and 5) exemptions to the
vaccination requirement. Other areas of discussion may include vaccination alternatives, such as testing
and/or masking, the length of time a vaccine mandate will be in effect and the basis for the policy, risk
factors considered, such as incidence rate of COVID-19 in the community and whether it applies to
employees only or all individuals entering a worksite. Lastly, employers can offer employees incentives to
get vaccines, but it cannot be so large that it is coercive.

Vaccine Mandates are Not Forced Medical Experiments or Human Testing

An employer cannot be criminally liable for mandating vaccines. Only the person who is primarily
responsible for the conduct of a medical experiment and who willfully fails to obtain the subject’s informed
consent and thereby exposes a subject to a known substantial risk of serious injury shall be guilty of a
misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment in the county jail for a period not to exceed one year or a fine of
fifty thousand dollars ($50,000), or both. (H&S Code § 24176.)

  Page 15 of 30
   Employees are not being forced to take the vaccine. They can freely choose not to take the vaccine.
  Moreover, the employer is not testing the vaccine on its employees. Human testing occurred before the
  vaccine was authorized for emergency use. Pfizer and other pharmaceutical companies tested vaccines on
  human subjects. Those human subjects gave their consent to be tested. An example of forced human
  testing would look like the following: co-workers come into your office, hold you down, and jab you with
  the vaccine without consent. That is not happening here. Your employer is mandating the vaccine to keep
  others safe. If you do not want to take the vaccine, you do not have to take the vaccine. However, the
  employer may terminate you because you are not abiding by the conditions of your employment.

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

x Engaged and Connected Residents
x Safe Community
x Attractive, Complementary Business District
x Beautiful, Preserved, Single-Family Neighborhoods

BACKGROUND

The San Marino High School Grad Night has been a long-standing tradition in the City for
generations. Planned and executed by volunteers, the Grad Night team coordinates all aspects of
this event and this involves design, assembly, and construction of various sets, stages, and props
necessary for the Grad Night Event which is held at San Marino High School.

The Grad Night Team has utilized the Wells Fargo parking facility at 2375 Huntington Drive for
the construction activities described above. The use of the parking facility at this location was
memorialized with a Parking Structure License Agreement between San Marino High School
Parent Teacher Student Association (PTA) which became effective January 2020 for a three-year
term.

On February 26, 2020 the Planning Commission granted a 90-day Temporary Use Permit (TUP)
for the Grad Night off site uses. The TUP is not an optimal planning tool for this activity. The
time limitations associated with the TUP requirements do not capture the amount of time
devoted to effectively design and fabricate the unique sets for the event. Nor does the TUP afford

  Page 17 of 30
 the Grad Night Team the flexibility to conduct all activities necessary to create a “custom
themed” event every year.

DISCUSSION

The attached draft ordinance proposes to amend sections of the C-1 Zone under “uses” to
identify this use and regulate it with some reasonable performance standards. The intent of the
draft ordinance is to provide some flexibility for this use to locate anywhere in the C-1 zone
where appropriate facilities exist. The performance standards are designed to ensure the use
operates in a manner that minimizes impacts on adjacent uses.

The draft ordinance was presented to the Planning Commission on October 27, 2021. There
were some questions about the proposed performance standards and their redundancy with
current standards in our code, questions about the ordinance format, and why we are codifying
a very specific community-based use. It was explained that the performance standards afford the
City additional protections wherever the use was to be conducted in the C-1 Zone and allow for
potential impacts to be ameliorated if necessary. In addition, the proposed text amendment
follows a similar format for all code text amendments. Lastly, it was explained that the use, while
being unique, could change or modify over time. For example, the group sponsoring Grad Night
could evolve or create other sub-groups for specific tasks and thereby still be subject to the
proposed standards.

After deliberating, the Planning Commission voted 5-0 to recommend to the City Council
adoption of the draft ordinance as presented.

At the November 10, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council voted 5-0 in favor of
introducing the ordinance on first reading.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

No fiscal impact is associated with this proposed action.

CEQA DETERMINATION

The subject code amendment is exempt from CEQA review under Section 15061(b)(3), the
general rule exemption. The proposed amendment has no potential of resulting in either a direct
physical change in the environment or a reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
environment. The proposed code amendment serves to establish performance standards for a
temporary use that occurs annually in conjunction with graduation celebration events for San
Marino High School, the use specifically involves storage, construction, and assembly of game
props. Pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3), the proposed amendment fits within the general rule that
CEQA only applies to projects that have the potential for causing a significant effect on the

  Page 18 of 30
 environment. In that the proposed amendment would provide clarity and streamline approval
process, the code amendment will not have a significant effect on the environment; and therefore,
the activity is not subject to CEQA.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney has reviewed and approved the staff report as to legal form.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the City Council adopt Ordinance No. O-21-1384. If the City Council concurs
with staff’s recommendation, an appropriate motion would be:

“I move to waive full reading, read by title only, and adopt Ordinance No. O-21-1384, an
Ordinance of the City of San Marino Amending the San Marino Municipal Code Sections 23.01.01
and 23.03.01 concerning Grad Night use in the C-1 Zone in the City of San Marino.”

SUBJECT:  APPROVAL OF ORDINANCE NO. O-21-1382 REGARDING THE
  PROHIBITION AND CITATION FOR FEEDING PEAFOWL
  (SECOND READING)

STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

x Engaged and Connected Residents
x Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
x Safe Community
x Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

In 2019, the City Council authorized the Peafowl Abatement Program, which included the
capturing and relocating of peafowl in the City. Over the past two years, the City and its vendor,
Wildlife Services, have captured and relocated close to 100 peafowl. Dozens of volunteer
homeowners helped the City and its vendor by participating in the program and allowing traps
to be set on their properties.

Although the program has been successful in controlling the peafowl population, it is clear and
evident that the remaining population continues to grow in specific concentrations in the City.
Through interviews with the public, it has been brought to our attention that a number of
property owners may be feeding the peafowl. Although staff has not witnessed these activities,
there are signs of feed on certain lawns. This issue seems to be more evident on Fairfield Place,
Gainsborough Drive, and Shakespeare Drive.

Cities such as Arcadia, Rancho Palos Verdes, and Rolling Hills Estates currently prohibit feeding
peafowl. These cities’ penalties for peafowl violations vary. For example, Arcadia imposes fines
of up to $1,000 per violation. Rancho Palos Verdes designates peafowl violations as infractions,
which results in a fine as small as $100 per violation.

The primary concern with fines is the enforcement process. In order to issue a citation or
perform criminal prosecution for these violations, the action of feeding the peafowl usually must

  Page 25 of 30
 be witnessed by a city official. If the action is not witnessed by a city official, an eyewitness must
agree to testify regarding the violation.

Despite the enforcement issues related to feeding peafowl, an ordinance prohibiting the feeding
of peafowl may be enough to deter such actions from occurring. Moreover, the amount of the
fine could also further deter this activity.

At the September 8, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council voted 3-2 in favor of introducing
the ordinance on first reading. At the November 10, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council
voted 5-0 in favor of introducing the ordinance on first reading with modifications. There was
some concern about the overly broad nature of the ordinance and some ambiguity regarding its
intent. Changes have been made to the ordinance to reflect clearly that the feeding of Peafowl is
prohibited.

DISCUSSION

Any violation of this provision will be deemed a public nuisance and may also be prosecuted as a
misdemeanor or be subject to the administrative citation process. By incorporating the public
nuisance language, the proposed amendment provides staff with a remedy for these violations via
an order to abate or for criminal prosecution. With the inclusion of the misdemeanor language,
the proposed amendment provides staff with the opportunity to issue an administrative citation
of up to $1,000. Depending on the severity of the violation, Code Enforcement staff will exercise
their discretion to use either tool necessary to abate the violation.

This Ordinance will go into effect 30 days from the date of adoption of this second reading. Staff
will undertake public outreach or education to inform residents of these changes.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

The adoption of this Ordinance may result in an increase to the City’s revenue under account
number 101-00-3410-0000, Fines and Fees.

LEGAL REVIEW

The City Attorney has reviewed and approved the staff report.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends the City Council adopt Ordinance No. O-21-1382. If the City Council concurs
with staff’s recommendation, an appropriate motion would be:

“I move to waive full reading, read by title only, and adopt Ordinance No. O-21-1382, an
Ordinance of the City of San Marino Amending the San Marino Municipal Code to Prohibit the
Feeding of Peafowl and to Amend the Administrative Citation Code to Include this Activity as a
Violation.”
